tracks.title: Where's the Board table?
tracks.text: Lesson 08 point 4 — boards. A sub-lesson, under workflows. And it starts with a search that comes back empty. Here's the instinct every tracker you've ever used has trained into you. A board is a second database. Somewhere there is a boards table… a columns schema… a card row with a status field… and a sync job whose whole life is dragging that database back toward reality after reality moves on. [curious] So go looking. Open this runtime and grep for it — Board structs, column models, a kanban service. The search is short. There is no Board table in the host. No card schema. No sync job — because there is nothing to sync between. The thing you expected to find… is the thing that was deliberately not built. And that absence isn't a gap. It's the design.

tracks.title: A board, decomposed
tracks.text: So here's the definition. A board is the kernel's render function — over the plan file — plus a write path back into that same file. Two verbs… zero models. Let me decompose that, because it's the whole trick. The read half is the kernel turning org into HTML. The write half is editing the file the HTML was rendered from. Nothing renders to a board… and nothing is stored as a board. The file is the single source, and a board is just a view of it that knows the way home. Picture the parent lesson's diagram, redrawn with the real function names on the arrows. At the center, one thing — plan dot org, the single source. From it, four arrows fan out, and three of them ride the same function, render. One goes to a kanban surface. One to a status page. One to a deadline calendar. And the fourth, riding a sibling function called tangle plan, goes to an agent's ready list. Then two dashed arrows curve back into the file — one labeled file write, P-U-T, from the kanban; one labeled file write, exec, from the ready list. The dashes are honest… we'll get to why. But notice what the picture is missing. There is no box in the middle holding state. No board between the file and its views. The runtime never learned what one is.

tracks.title: The one-line denial
tracks.text: Next — the one-line denial. You don't have to take the diagram's word for it, because the runtime says it out loud, in the very module you'd expect to find a board inside. Here is the moduledoc, read as written. A workflow is the unit of orchestration — there is no separate board. A native org workflow headline is the D-A-G. Org owns the orchestration spec… the runtime just executes it — no D-S-L, no board model. [curious] Grep the whole host layer for the word board, and you find it in only three kinds of place. First, that denial. Second, the names of org files — plan dot org, board dot org — that some agents generate. Third, one module whose job is to write an org file… not to model a board. No struct. No table. No schema. This is the host-versus-loaded boundary showing through. The host holds primitives — parse, render, run. A board is product behavior, and product behavior lives in the declarative layer. It's org text and a little C-S-S, not engine code. The runtime can't drift from a board model… for the same reason it can't have a bug in one. It doesn't have one.

tracks.title: One line of Rust, three surfaces
tracks.text: Now a depth rung — the read half, all the way down. And it really is one line. The kernel declares a single export in its interface type… render… a function from string to string. Every export is string to string, and the kernel takes no host imports at all — which is its own kind of safety. Hand it anything but a string and the fault traps inside the WebAssembly runtime before it touches a thing. And the body behind that export? Here it is, in full. Pub fn render, taking an org string, returns a string… by calling Org parse on it… then to H-T-M-L. That's it. Parse the org, emit the HTML. The heavy lifting is borrowed — orgize, an open-source org parser — so the kernel's own contribution is a function you can read in one breath. [excited] And because it's that small and that pure, the same function reaches three surfaces with no second copy. Picture one function at the left — crate render — fanning into three. First, a wasm Component, which becomes the runtime page you get at slash w slash i-d. Second, a browser ABI over pointer and length, which is how this very learn notebook renders org with no server at all. Third, a native rlib, which is the command-line tool. Three exits… one function. As the kernel source itself puts it — there is no wasm version of the logic. One body, three wrappers.

tracks.title: The page that talks back
tracks.text: Rendering gives you a board you can look at. What makes it a board you can use… is that the served page ships with a way home. The runtime hands every workbook page a tiny client — window dot w-b — pointed back at the same engine that rendered it. Read it as written. Window dot w-b has two methods. Call — which fetches slash w slash i-d slash call. And live — which opens a WebSocket to slash w slash i-d slash w-s. And the comment beside it… the Workbook U-I talks to its backend — this same runtime. So the full loop is four arrows between a browser and one runtime, against one file. Walk it. First, the browser P-U-T-s the org source up… and the runtime answers 201 stored. Second, the browser G-E-T-s the rendered page back… and gets the page plus that window dot w-b client. Third, the page calls home — w-b dot call validate, over H-T-T-P. Fourth, the page streams — w-b dot live render, over the socket, with frames that are just fn and org. The H-T-T-P endpoint dispatches a small verb set — parse, tangle, validate — straight into the kernel. The socket adds render to the same dispatch and streams it — its own moduledoc calls it the interactive upgrade over the H-T-T-P backend, same dispatch, streamed. Either way… the page and its backend cannot disagree, because they are the same runtime reading the same file you P-U-T.

tracks.title: The board is the runner, paused
tracks.text: Here's the cleanest proof that the board and the execution are one thing. The runtime exposes a single workflow endpoint… with a flag. Add plan equals one, and it returns the schedule — the board view, no execution. Drop the flag, and it runs the same plan. And both branches start from the identical kernel call — tangle plan. The board is literally the dry-run of the runner. Let me read the two side by side. With plan equals one, you post the org and get back a list… one workflow, its schedule with an at-time and a repeat, its tasks by name, its sub-workflows. Nothing runs. Without the flag, you post the org plus an input… and get the same shape — but now the tasks carry outputs, exports are surfaced, and the steps actually executed. So picture a tiny table, two columns — plan, and run. The kernel call? Same in both — tangle plan. What comes back? The same shape — except run adds the task outputs. What actually runs? In the plan column… nothing, just the schedule. In the run column… every step, in topological waves. That last phrase matters. Execution order isn't configured anywhere. A wave is the set of steps whose predecessors are all done… and steps inside a wave are independent, so they run in parallel. The plan view is that exact computation… with the running switched off. You're never looking at a different artifact than the one that executes. You're looking at it… at rest.

tracks.title: A status page that is two file reads
tracks.text: Another depth rung — a status page that is two file reads. A live board, the thing that shows you a run clearing in real time, sounds like it must need a stateful server pushing card updates. It doesn't. Watch the lifecycle of the TODO runner, where the native org outline is the state machine — no custom tags, the keywords are the columns. Picture the sequence. First, the client posts the org outline to slash api slash workflow slash todo. Second, the runtime writes a one-line status file — slug, and stage running — then answers 202, running, immediately, and spawns the runner in the background. Third, while the runner works, the client polls a status endpoint… and that endpoint is nothing but File dot read of status dot json. On finish, the runner overwrites the file with stage done and the task list. On a crash… stage error. Here it is in three curls. First, post the outline — back comes 202, slug w-f 42 17, running. Second, curl the status — mid-run it reads stage running… and after, stage done, with a task list where each task has an id, an index, a title, a state of DONE, an output, and a timestamp. Third, curl the telemetry — stage done, the tasks, 23 tool calls, 48 thousand milliseconds total, no errors. That telemetry endpoint reads two files — status dot json for the stage and tasks, and steps dot j-s-o-n-l, a line per tool call written at the chokepoint every exec agent passes through. [excited] It's observable mid-flight precisely because there is no board object to query. The truth is on disk… and a status page is just someone reading it. And the minimum-viable kanban? Three C-S-S lines in the runtime's own viewer. K-W TODO paints red. K-W DONE paints green. K-W NEXT and WAIT paint amber. A little JavaScript lifts each headline's leading keyword into a badge. That's the entire board styling — semantics from the file… layout from your stylesheet.

tracks.title: The agent is a board consumer
tracks.text: There's a third board… and it has no pixels. It's the ready set an agent reads to decide what to do next. The TODO runner treats the org outline as the whole specification — keywords are states, nesting is sub-workflows, ordering and edges are properties — and the agent consumes it the way a worker reads a board. Walk the mapping. A TODO or NEXT or DOING keyword is the card's column. A TODO whose dependencies are all DONE is ready — pick it up. Nesting is a sub-workflow. The property ordered, set true, means siblings run in sequence… and its absence means they run in parallel, up to eight at once. A blocker property is an explicit cross-edge. A done-when clause, or a check block, is the gate that lets a card reach DONE. And an already-DONE headline is the resume cursor — skipped on rerun. Two of those carry more than they look. DONE is not a free claim — a task with a done-when shell command, or a check block, only reaches DONE if that check passes… and it runs in the wasm shell, fail-closed, never on the native host. And because already-DONE tasks are skipped, the file's own states are the resume cursor. Kill a run, restart it, and it picks up exactly where the file says the work stopped. The board isn't a view of the agent's progress. It's the surface the agent reads… mutates… and resumes from — all in one file.

tracks.title: Boards running in production
tracks.text: This isn't a thought experiment. Real standing agents work real boards through this exact seam, every day. Three of them — and the contrast between them is the lesson. Think of a small table, three rows. First row — plan dot org, the keeper's board. It reads from its own backlog, it writes back — pick up becomes NEXT, put down becomes TODO, cancel becomes CANCELLED — and the direction is two-way. Second row — dream verdicts. They read from the last run's telemetry, they write back mechanical edits to plan dot org, also two-way. Third row — board dot org, the groundskeeper's. It reads from the bd task store, it is never hand-edited, and its direction is one-way… by choice. Now the story behind the table. The keeper that tends this project's landing site runs in plan mode by default — the agent only critiques and updates its backlog, it never edits the page directly. Its plan dot org is a standing board that, in the lifecycle's own words, is the ongoing task D-A-G — it never completes. Each night, the dream phase writes back into it through a deliberately mechanical protocol — a verdict must name the exact heading text of a task on the board, and the agent applies it by rule. That's a real agent exercising the write half… nightly. And the counter-example is the instructive one. Board dot org is regenerated from the bd store in one direction, grouped by priority — and its own header says it. Never hand-edited, no two-way sync. That's not a limitation of the architecture. It's a surface that chose to be read-only, because its truth lives elsewhere. [curious] Direction is per-surface policy… not a property of boards. Which is exactly the freedom this design buys you.

tracks.title: Where it bites
tracks.text: Now the honest part — where it bites. The clean story has real edges, and you should know them before you build on it. First… the R-P-C seam is read-only. The call and socket verbs are parse, tangle, validate, render — all reads. There is no set-state verb, no flip-to-DONE. Mutation today means writing the file — an agent with exec, a human with an editor, or a P-U-T. The parent's drag-a-card-to-the-file picture is the architecture's affordance… not a shipped widget. Second… there is no drag-drop kanban in the repo. None ships. The keyword badges in the viewer are the pattern at minimum scale, and a full board is yours to build on the seam. Third… render gives you semantics, not layout. It emits generic HTML with keyword classes. Columns, swimlanes, drag handles — that's your C-S-S and JavaScript over those states. Fourth… the live board lives in slash t-m-p. The status and step files are ephemeral by design. Durable history is the sealed ledger and the SQLite telemetry database, not the tmp files a poll reads. And fifth… one-way is a choice you must make on purpose. Nothing stops two writers fighting over one file. Board dot org avoids that by declaring itself generated-only. None of these is a missing feature pretending to be a principle. The design gives you the two verbs and the one file… what you render, and which way you let it flow, it deliberately leaves to you.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] So how do I flip a card to DONE? You edit the file. Change the headline's keyword to DONE and P-U-T the new source — or let an agent with exec do it. There is no flip-a-card endpoint, because the file is the card. Can I build a real kanban on this? Yes — you have both halves. For columns, call render, or tangle plan if you want structured tasks, and group by keyword. For writes, P-U-T the edited org back. A richer board is more stylesheet, not more engine. Why isn't there a mutation API? Because the file is the API. A set-state R-P-C would be a second writer to a thing that already has one good way to be written… and a second writer is exactly how a board drifts. Isn't board dot org a contradiction — a one-way board? No. Direction is policy, not architecture. Two-way is available… one-way was chosen. Both are boards. And does this scale past t-m-p? The live view is meant to be ephemeral — cheap to read, fine to lose. Durable truth is the plan file in version control, plus the ledger and the telemetry database. [chuckles] Don't treat the tmp files as the record. Treat them as the window.

tracks.title: Back up to the parent
tracks.text: So that's boards. Not a database with views… a rendering. The kernel's render function over the plan file, plus a write path home — two verbs, zero models, and a runtime that can't drift from a board because it never learned what one is. [curious] The way back up is short. This sub-lesson stands on its parent — workflows, lesson eight, the plan a board renders. And it leans on org, the grammar render understands, and agents, who hold the ready list. Everything a board does… is built from those. Next time you reach for a tracker, you'll notice the second database hiding inside it. Here, there isn't one. There's just the file… and the way home.
